implementation_notes: TypeScript adds the discipline of a required parameter: the client is written to take an AbortSignal (op: (signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<T>), so every call site must supply a budget, and AbortSignal.timeout(ms) - declared in lib.dom and in the Node type definitions - produces a signal that aborts with a TimeoutError DOMException; AbortSignal.any([callerSignal, timeoutSignal]) composes the deadline with caller cancellation into one signal that fetch, streams and HTTP clients accept. Availability is a lib/target question: an older lib or @types/node declares neither AbortSignal.timeout nor any(), and the values then have to be supplied by hand. The typed wrapper should translate the DOMException into the project's own error type so callers narrow on a domain error instead of matching a string name.
pitfalls: The signal is only advisory: an API whose type takes no AbortSignal cannot be bounded, and a wrapper type does not change that at runtime.
TimeoutError exists only as a DOMException name here, so without a translation the rest of the code has to match on error names rather than on types.
Promise<T> looks identical whether or not the underlying work was cancelled, so a typed helper must document that a timed-out operation may still complete.

variants.name: Generic promise-race wrapper for APIs without a signal
variants.implementation_notes: When the callee's type offers no AbortSignal parameter, the typed realization is a generic wrapper around Promise.race: it races the promise against a rejecting timer, clears the timer on settle and keeps the result type T intact. The signature deliberately cannot express cancellation, so the wrapper must document that the operation continues in the background - which is why this variant is a fallback and not the default. Combining it with the signal variant at the boundary (the wrapper creates a controller it forwards to clients that accept one) is what makes it safe in practice.
pitfalls: The losing promise keeps running: the wrapper bounds the await, not the operation, so the caller may observe side effects later.
setTimeout returns a Node Timeout object or a number depending on the lib target, so typing the handle wrongly breaks clearTimeout under @types/node.
A late rejection from the abandoned promise becomes an unhandled rejection in strict runtimes unless a catch is attached before the race.
